questions.question: State and prove the work-energy theorem for a constant force.
questions.solution:
**Work-energy theorem:** The work done by the net force on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy.

Proof: Let a constant force F act on mass m, producing acceleration a. From v² = u² + 2as:

W = F·s = (ma)s = m(a·s). Since as = (v² − u²)/2,

W = m(v² − u²)/2 = ½mv² − ½mu² = ΔKE.

Thus work done = change in kinetic energy. Proved.
questions.knowledgeNote: The theorem holds for ALL forces — conservative and non-conservative alike.
questions.answer: **Statement:** net work done on a body = change in kinetic energy: **W_net = ½mv² − ½mu²**. **Proof (constant force):** with net force F over displacement s, Newton's second law gives F = ma, and the equation of motion v² = u² + 2as gives a = (v² − u²)/(2s). Substituting: W = Fs = m(v² − u²)/(2s) × s = ½mv² − ½mu² = ΔKE. ∎ **Deep point:** one substitution proves it — kinematics' 'a' dropped into dynamics' 'F = ma'; the theorem needs only end-point speeds, which is why it outlives every detail of the force's schedule.

questions.question: An electric motor has a power output of 2 kW. How much time will it take to lift a 500 kg mass through 20 m? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.knowledgeNote: Power = Work/Time; 1 W = 1 J/s and 1 HP = 746 W.
questions.answer: **Work:** W = mgh = 500 × 10 × 20 = 100 000 J. **Time:** t = W/P = 100 000/2000 = **50 s**. **Deep point:** energy first, time second — P = W/t is the whole machine; with g = 9.8 the answer would be 49 s, so quote the g you used.

questions.question: Calculate the work done in stretching a spring of force constant 200 N/m by 0.1 m from its unstretched position.
questions.solution:
Work stored as elastic potential energy: W = ½kx².

W = ½ × 200 × (0.1)² = 100 × 0.01 = **1 J**.
questions.knowledgeNote: Spring work goes as x² — doubling the stretch quadruples the stored energy.
questions.answer: **Elastic PE:** W = ½kx² = ½ × 200 × (0.1)² = ½ × 200 × 0.01 = **1 J**. **Deep point:** the ½ is the F–x triangle — force ramps 0 → kx during the stretch, so the work is half of kx × x; forgetting it doubles the answer.

questions.question: Show that the total mechanical energy of a freely falling body is conserved (neglect air resistance).
questions.solution:
Drop mass m from height H. At height h with velocity v, energy conservation from rest gives v² = 2g(H − h).

KE + PE = ½mv² + mgh = ½m·2g(H − h) + mgh = mgH − mgh + mgh = **mgH = constant**.

At the top (h = H) it is all potential; at the ground (h = 0) it is all kinetic — the sum never changes.
questions.knowledgeNote: Only conservative forces (gravity, spring) conserve mechanical energy; friction converts part of it to heat.
questions.answer: **Conservation of mechanical energy (free fall):** take the body of mass m at height h (at rest) and let it fall. **At the top:** KE = 0, PE = mgh ⟹ total E = mgh. **After falling distance x** (height h − x, speed v): PE = mg(h − x); KE from v² = 2gx: KE = ½m(2gx) = mgx. **Total:** E = mg(h − x) + mgx = **mgh** — unchanged. **At the ground:** PE = 0, KE = ½mv² = ½m(2gh) = mgh ⟹ E = mgh again. The total mechanical energy is **mgh at every point** of the fall (loss in PE = gain in KE at every stage), so it is conserved when air resistance is neglected. **Deep point:** the proof is the bookkeeping identity PE loss = KE gain — v² = 2gx is the only physics input, and it is itself the work–energy theorem for gravity.

questions.question: A car of mass 1000 kg moves at a uniform speed of 20 m/s against a total resistive force of 500 N. What power must the engine develop?
questions.solution:
At uniform speed the driving force equals the resistance: F = 500 N.

P = F·v = 500 × 20 = 10,000 W = **10 kW**.
questions.knowledgeNote: For steady motion P = Fv — the same form as W = F·s divided by time.
questions.answer: **Uniform speed ⟹ net force balances resistance:** the engine's driving force F = 500 N. **Power:** P = Fv = 500 × 20 = **10 000 W = 10 kW**. **Deep point:** P = Fv is the working form of P = W/t for steady motion — at constant speed all engine power goes against the resistance, none into accelerating; that's why highway power demand is a drag-and-speed product.

questions.question: Define the kilowatt-hour (kWh). How many joules are equal to 1 kWh?
questions.solution:
**1 kWh** is the energy consumed by a 1 kW appliance running for 1 hour (the commercial 'unit' of electrical energy).

1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = **3.6 × 10⁶ J**.
questions.knowledgeNote: kWh is a unit of ENERGY, not power — a classic one-mark NEB trap.
questions.answer: **Kilowatt-hour:** the commercial **unit of electrical energy** — the energy consumed when power is used at the rate of **1 kilowatt for 1 hour**; it is an energy unit, not a power unit, and is what electricity meters and bills count. **Conversion:** 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = **3.6 × 10⁶ J** (3.6 MJ). **Deep point:** the kWh survives because it is human-scaled — a 1 kWh unit runs a 1 kW heater for an hour; in joules that same energy is awkwardly large, which is why bills never say 'joules'.
